notes.label: Interwoven word order
notes.trans: with mighty strength ... a huge spear
notes.body: validis ... viribus and ingentem ... hastam are interlaced, so the strength and the spear are woven together, which makes the throw sound powerful.

notes.label: Hyperbaton
notes.body: curvam and alvum are split by compagibus, so the timbers sit inside the belly, just as the Greeks sit inside the horse.

notes.label: Enjambment
notes.body: contorsit runs over to the start of line 52 after two lines of build-up, so the throw lands with force at the beginning of the line.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: stetit comes straight after the colon, so the reader pictures the spear stopping dead in the wood.

notes.label: Word choice
notes.body: uterus means "womb", so the horse is pictured as pregnant with the soldiers inside it, a grim image of what will be "born" from it.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: insonuere opens the line, so the echo of the hollow horse is the first thing we hear.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: cavernae is held back to the end of the sentence, so the hollows that could have given the Greeks away are the last word.

notes.label: Assonance
notes.body: The repeated cav- sound in cavae ... cavernae imitates the hollow booming of the horse, so the reader can almost hear it.

notes.label: Anaphora
notes.trans: if the fates ..., if our minds
notes.body: si is repeated at the start of each condition, which stresses the two things that went wrong: the will of the gods and the Trojans' own blindness.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: impulerat opens the line, so Laocoön's action is stressed: he came very close to saving Troy.

notes.label: Indicative
notes.body: The indicative impulerat is used where a subjunctive is expected, which shows how nearly it happened: Laocoön had all but driven them to it.

notes.label: Hyperbaton
notes.body: Argolicas and latebras are split by foedare, so the act of tearing open sits inside the Greeks' hiding place.

notes.label: Apostrophe
notes.body: Aeneas turns to speak directly to Priam's citadel, which shows his grief and lets the reader feel the loss of Troy.

notes.label: Argive
notes.body: From Argos, a leading Greek city; Virgil uses Argolicus to mean simply "Greek".

notes.label: Priam
notes.body: Priam was the old king of Troy. Aeneas, who is telling the story, belonged to a junior branch of the royal family.

questions: What does the sound of the spear striking the horse suggest to the reader, and why do the Trojans not notice?
In lines 54–56 Aeneas imagines what might have been. What does this tell us about his feelings as he tells the story?

context.body: Lines 54 to 56 are a moment of "if only". Aeneas is telling the story years later at Dido's court, and he knows that Troy fell. He blames two things: the fates set by the gods, and the Trojans' own folly. This mix of divine will and human blindness runs through the whole of Book 2: the gods want Troy to fall, but the Trojans also make their own fatal choices.
